extra.message: SQLAlchemy echo=True logs all queries including sensitive user data

In production (containerized deployment), stdout becomes the container log, making all user data persistently stored in log files accessible to anyone with log access.

extra.message: Missing rate limiting on POST /login allows brute-force password attacks

extra.message: Missing @login_required on POST /darkmode allows unauthenticated cookie writes

extra.message: Preferences cookie set without Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite attributes in toggle_darkmode

metadata.proof: The set_cookie() call at line 107 has no Secure=True, HttpOnly=True, or SameSite='Lax'/'Strict' parameters. The cookie is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP (no Secure flag), accessible to JavaScript via document.cookie (no HttpOnly flag — amplified by existing XSS at templates/home.html:34), and sent cross-origin on POST requests (no SameSite flag). Combined with the pickle-serialized payload, this enables session-level attacks including cookie theft via XSS and CSRF-assisted pickle deserialization RCE.

extra.message: Sensitive user email exposed via /is_logged_in endpoint without authentication

metadata.proof: The GET /is_logged_in route (line 47) returns current_user.email in the JSON response at line 52 without requiring @login_required. A malicious site can make a cross-origin fetch to GET /is_logged_in and, if the victim has an active session, receive the victim's email address. extra.message: Missing rate limiting on POST /notes enables unrestricted note flood and resource exhaustion

metadata.proof: The POST /notes handler (lines 16-30) accepts user-supplied title, text, and private flag with no throttling, CAPTCHA, or per-user creation limits. An authenticated attacker can programmatically send thousands of note-creation requests per second. Each request inserts a row into the SQLite database (session.add/commit at lines 27-29), growing database.db without bound. The unbounded note retrieval in utils/notes.py:10 (CWE-770) amplifies this — every user loading /home buffers ALL public notes into memory.

extra.message: Missing rate limiting on POST /account/image enables server-side request flooding

metadata.proof: The POST /account/image handler accepts a user-supplied URL with no throttling, per-user limits, or CAPTCHA. Each request triggers urlopen() (utils/profile_image.py:7) to an arbitrary URL. An attacker can submit thousands of requests per second, enabling: (1) amplification DDoS attacks against third-party servers; (2) exhaustion of the server's file descriptor/connection pool; (3) rapid filling of the SQLite database with base64 blobs via the profile_image BLOB column. Combined with CWE-918 (SSRF), the missing rate limit turns a targeted SSRF into a high-throughput attack tool.

extra.message: Newly generated registration code value exposed in flash message returned in HTTP response

metadata.proof: When an admin POSTs to /registration-codes, a new RegistrationCode is generated with a fresh UUID at line 34, and the plaintext code value is interpolated into a flash message at line 38. The flash message is rendered into the next HTTP response (registration_codes.html via bootstrap render_messages). The registration code value appears in the HTML body, where it can be: (1) intercepted over plain HTTP (no HTTPS); (2) cached by intermediate proxies; (3) read by browser extensions or XSS payloads. Registration codes are secret invite tokens — exposing them in the clear defeats their purpose as access controls.

extra.message: Preferences cookie set without Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite in after_request handler

metadata.proof: In the after_request hook at lines 125-131, when a first-time visitor has no preferences cookie, a default preferences dict is serialized via pickle and set as a cookie with no Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite attributes. This fires on every unauthenticated request, meaning every attacker probing the server receives a pickle-serialized cookie over plain HTTP with no protections. While the content is benign {'mode': 'light'}, the attacker learns: (1) the exact serialization format (pickle + base64); (2) that any manipulated cookie blob will be deserialized on the next request (before_request at line 120). This acts as an oracle confirming the pickle deserialization attack surface (CWE-502) with zero authentication.

extra.message: CSV Formula Injection via exported personal notes table

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Note text is fully user-controlled (created via POST /notes with CKEditor, stored in DB without sanitization). SINK: The render_table call at line 16 renders note text as raw HTML via safe_columns=['text']. The client-side CSV export JavaScript (lines 29-62) reads cell content via innerText, double-quote-escapes only CSV delimiters (line 37), and wraps in quotes (line 39). When note text starts with =, +, -, or @ (e.g. =cmd|'/c calc'!A0), the resulting CSV cell is "=cmd|...", which Excel/Google Sheets interprets as an executable formula upon opening — the double-quote wrapping alone does not prevent formula interpretation.

extra.message: Password change does not invalidate existing Flask-Login sessions

metadata.proof: SOURCE: A user or attacker (via CSRF at line 68) changes their password via POST /account. SINK: Only the DB password hash is updated at line 87-89. No call to logout_user() or session-revocation mechanism follows. Flask-Login authenticates via a signed cookie containing the user ID; load_user (routes/login.py:8-10) reloads by ID without checking password currency. A stolen session cookie remains valid indefinitely after password change, allowing continued attacker access even after the victim resets credentials.

extra.message: Registration codes (bearer tokens) stored in plaintext in the database

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Registration codes are generated as random UUIDs via str(uuid4()) at routes/registration_codes.py:40 and function as bearer tokens for account creation. SINK: They are stored in plaintext via String column (line 12) with no hashing, salting, or encryption. The SQL injection vulnerability at routes/account.py:33 allows an authenticated attacker to extract all valid registration codes from the registration_code table (e.g. UNION SELECT code FROM registration_code--), bypassing the invitation-only signup gate entirely. Even without SQLi, any direct DB access (SQLite file read) exposes all codes.

extra.message: Registration codes have no expiration and persist indefinitely until used

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The add_registration_codes handler at line 40 instantiates a RegistrationCode with no expiry timestamp or TTL parameter. SINK: No expiry duration is set on the RegistrationCode model (models/registration_code.py:12 has only 'code' and inherited 'created_at' fields), and no TTL check exists in validate_token (routes/signup.py:21-28) or do_signup (routes/signup.py:49-62). Codes remain valid forever until explicitly consumed by a successful signup, which deletes the used token (line 62). A code generated on day one is equally valid years later, expanding the window for brute-force guessing or credential-stuffing of code values against POST /signup.

extra.message: Unbounded note query with no pagination enables memory exhaustion

metadata.proof: SOURCE: get_notes_for_user is called by routes/home.py:15 and routes/notes.py:14 with the current user's ID. SINK: The query at line 9-11 returns ALL matching rows (user's own notes + all non-private notes from every other user) via .all() with no .limit() or pagination. In a populated instance, this can return thousands of Note objects, each eagerly loaded with its User relationship (joinedload). A single HTTP request to /home or /notes forces the server to materialize the entire result set into memory, allowing resource-exhaustion DoS by any authenticated user.

extra.message: Unbounded personal-notes query with no pagination enables resource exhaustion

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The user_id from the URL path /accounts/<int:user_id>/notes is used directly in the filter, with no authorization check (IDOR, CWE-639 — any authenticated user can target any user_id). SINK: The .all() call at line 46 returns every note (private and public) belonging to that user with no LIMIT clause. An attacker can request notes for the user with the most notes, forcing the server to allocate memory for an unbounded result set. No pagination or row cap exists.
